stem: A bond has a modified duration of 7.20. Its yield to maturity rises by 25 basis points. Ignoring convexity, the percentage change in the bond's price is closest to:
solution: The first order approximation is minus modified duration multiplied by the change in yield: -7.20 x 0.0025 = -0.0180, a fall of 1.80%. Ignoring convexity slightly overstates the loss, because the price yield curve is convex.
distractors: This divides rather than multiplies, 0.0025 / 7.20 x 100.
This has the sign the wrong way round. A rise in yield lowers price.

stem: An annual-pay bond has a Macaulay duration of 6.50 years and a yield to maturity of 4.0%. Its modified duration is closest to:
solution: Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by one plus the yield per period: 6.50 / 1.04 = 6.25. Modified duration is always the smaller of the two for a positive yield.
distractors: This is the Macaulay duration itself, undiscounted.
This multiplies by 1.04 instead of dividing, which moves in the wrong direction.

stem: The one-year spot rate is 3.00% and the two-year spot rate is 4.00%, both annually compounded. The one-year rate implied one year forward is closest to:
solution: No arbitrage requires that investing for two years at the two-year spot equals investing for one year and rolling at the forward rate. So (1.04)^2 / 1.03 - 1 = 1.0816 / 1.03 - 1 = 5.01%. The forward rate sits above the two-year spot because the spot curve is upward sloping.
distractors: This is roughly the average of the two spot rates and reflects no compounding relationship.
This interpolates between the spot rates rather than solving the no arbitrage condition. The forward must exceed the longer spot on an upward sloping curve.
